notes:
Now let me compile the verse-by-verse notes from the material I've gathered across traditions.

---

## 1 Kings 2:1-23 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

---

### v. 1 — *"As the time drew near for David to die, he charged his son Solomon…"*

- **Traditional reading**: This is a private deathbed charge, distinct from the public farewell address David gave earlier (1 Chronicles 28–29). The solemnity of a dying father's words is in view, though all commentators note the authority of a living God far surpasses even this. (JFB, via StudyLight.org excerpts; Matthew Henry's Concise Commentary)
  - URL: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfb/1-kings-2.html
  - URL: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/mhn/1-kings-2.html

- **Ellicott** notes that between chapters 1 and 2, the Chronicler records a great assembly of princes and a "second" anointing of Solomon (1 Chronicles 29:22), possibly representing formal acceptance by all the tribes. David "stood up on his feet" for that occasion (1 Chronicles 28:2), suggesting the excitement renewed his strength temporarily.
  - URL: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_kings/2.htm

- **Pulpit Commentary**: The words echo Joshua 23–24. The thought of Joshua may have suggested the next words ("be strong"). David was unquestionably well-versed in the Scriptures of his age.
  - URL: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/1_kings/2.htm

---

### v. 2 — *"I am about to go the way of all the earth. So be strong and prove yourself a man."*

- **Traditional reading**: "The way of all the earth" is a beautiful, impressive periphrasis for death — the path to Sheol all mankind treads. (JFB; Pulpit). David, Israel's greatest king short of the Messiah, recognized he was but a man sharing the common destiny of all. (Enduring Word)
  - URL: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-2/
  - URL: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/1_kings/2.htm

- **"Be strong… prove yourself a man"** : David likely sensed some weakness in Solomon. The same expression was used by the Philistines in 1 Samuel 4:9 as they encouraged one another in battle. Great responsibilities require great strength and courage. (Enduring Word)
  - URL: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-2/

- **JFB** compares this counsel to the apostolic direction in 1 Corinthians 16:13, referring to fortitude of mind required for the onerous functions of a king.
  - URL: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfb/1-kings-2.html

- **Ellicott**: "I go the way of all the earth" — compare Joshua 23:14.
  - URL: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_kings/2.htm

- **Pulpit** notes that similar words were addressed four times to Joshua (Joshua 1:6, 7, 9, 18). Solomon's age at accession is uncertain: Josephus says fourteen, Eupolemus twelve. The Pulpit commentator inclines to think the words "young and tender" (1 Chronicles 22:5) argue against the common view that he was about twenty.
  - URL: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/1_kings/2.htm

---

### v. 3 — *"And keep the charge of the LORD your God to walk in His ways and to keep His statutes, commandments, ordinances, and decrees, as is written in the Law of Moses, so that you may prosper in all you do and wherever you turn…"*

- **Traditional reading**: David knew Solomon could not be strong or courageous without obedient fellowship with God. The four terms — statutes, commandments, ordinances/judgments, testimonies — are an accumulation of practically synonymous terms representing the totality of the Law (Keil, cited in Pulpit). The phrase is derived from the Pentateuch.
  - URL: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-2/
  - URL: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/1_kings/2.htm

- **Ellicott**: The main charge is noble — show yourself a man despite youth, follow the Law, trust in God's promises. It accords with "the last words of David" (2 Samuel 23:3-5) and with David's prayer in 1 Chronicles 29:18-19. In all this David speaks in the spirit of a true servant and saint of God.
  - URL: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_kings/2.htm

- **"Prosper"** (or "do wisely"): The Pulpit Commentary notes that the marginal "do wisely" is preferred by some (Keil), but the translation "prosper" has the weight of Gesenius and fits the context better — the end sought is not merely acting wisely but receiving the blessing of success (cf. Joshua 1:7).
  - URL: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/1_kings/2.htm

- **JFB**: "Keep the charge of the LORD thy God" refers to the divine law in all its ceremonial and moral requirements, but particularly the political institutions for the Hebrew monarch (Deuteronomy 17:10-20).
  - URL: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfb/1-kings-2.html

- **StudyLight.org (Keil & Delitzsch)** : The phrase "keep the keeping of Jehovah" always receives its precise definition from context, here denoting obedience to the law of God in all its extent.
  - URL: https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-kings/2-1.html

---

### v. 4 — *"…so that the LORD may fulfill His promise to me: 'If your descendants take heed to walk faithfully before Me with all their heart and soul, you will never fail to have a man on the throne of Israel.'"*

- **Traditional reading**: This refers to the Davidic Covenant (2 Samuel 7:12-16). In the original promise through Nathan, the conditional "if" clause was not explicitly stated, but here and in 1 Kings 8:25 and 9:5, the condition is given prominence. It was no doubt understood, if not expressed, when the promise was first made.
  - URL: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/1_kings/2.htm
  - URL: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-2/

- **Reformed / Baptist view (John Piper, Desiring God)** : The conditionality of the covenant is repeated again and again: "as long as David's sons are disobedient the kingdom cannot be made secure forever." This points forward to the need for a perfectly obedient Son of David — Christ. The promise was absolute concerning the Messiah; conditional concerning the temporal throne.
  - URL: https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/gods-covenant-with-david

- **Matthew Henry**: "God promised David that the Messiah should come from his descendants, and that promise was absolute; but the promise, that there should not fail of them a man on the throne of Israel, was conditional — if he walks before God in sincerity, with zeal and resolution."
  - URL: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/mhn/1-kings-2.html

- **Enduring Word (David Guzik)** : We may envy the sons of David for having such a promise, but we have a similar promise from God: "Seek first the kingdom of God and His righteousness, and all these things shall be added to you" (Matthew 6:33).
  - URL: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-2/

- **Pulpit Commentary**: The thought that the permanence of the dynasty depended on faithful observance of the Law seems to have reminded the dying king that *he himself* had not always kept the statutes — particularly regarding unpunished murder. This prompts the specific charges that follow.
  - URL: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/1_kings/2.htm

---

### v. 5 — *"Moreover, you know what Joab son of Zeruiah did to me—what he did to Abner son of Ner and Amasa son of Jether…"*

- **Traditional reading**: David charges Solomon concerning Joab's treacherous murders of Abner (2 Samuel 3:27) and Amasa (2 Samuel 20:9-10). He describes these as shedding "the blood of war in peacetime" — blood that might lawfully be shed in fair fight, but Joab killed these men by treachery when they were at peace with him.
  - URL: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-2/
  - URL: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/1_kings/2.htm

- **Pulpit Commentary** stresses that David is careful *not* to include his private wrongs; the "what Joab did to me" is because "the sovereign is smitten in the subject" (Bishop Hall). David's motive is not personal revenge but the administration of divine justice under the Mosaic law. The horrific details of the blood spurting on Joab's girdle and sandals had made a deep impression on David's mind.
  - URL: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/1_kings/2.htm

- **Ellicott**: The charge as to Joab "has a certain righteousness in it." David could not — probably since Joab knew of his great crime with Uriah — punish him. Yet Ellicott notes David makes no mention of the act for which he probably bore the most grudge: Joab's reckless slaughter of Absalom against David's express command. Nor does he mention Joab's recent treason (supporting Adonijah), which had likely already embittered Solomon against him.
  - URL: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_kings/2.htm

- **Enduring Word** suggests many think David did not command Joab's execution during his lifetime because Joab knew about the murder of Uriah (2 Samuel 11:14-25) — that Joab used this knowledge as blackmail. Yet others knew too (Nathan, servants), so this may not fully explain David's inaction. More likely, "David felt under obligation to Joab" for years of loyalty and could not cope with the mixture of Joab's loyalty and misdeeds.
  - URL: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-2/

---

### v. 6 — *"So act according to your wisdom, and do not let his gray head go down to Sheol in peace."*

- **Traditional reading**: "Do not let his gray head go down to Sheol in peace" means Joab must die a violent death, not a natural one. It needed great discretion (wisdom) to execute one so powerful, so connected to the army, whose crimes had been passed over so long, and to whom David owed so much. To act rashly might provoke a revolution.
  - URL: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/1_kings/2.htm

- **Pulpit Commentary** defends David against the charge of vindictiveness: under the Old Testament dispensation of temporal rewards and punishments, the Mosaic code was a *lex talionis* demanding blood for blood. The king had no power to pardon murder. The land itself was defiled until justice was done (Numbers 35:33). David had seen his country visited by famine because of unavenged blood (the Gibeonites, 2 Samuel 21:1). Joab's execution was a matter of covenantal justice, not personal malice.
  - URL: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/1_kings/2.htm

---

### v. 7 — *"But show loving devotion to the sons of Barzillai the Gileadite, and let them be among those who eat at your table, because they stood by me when I fled from your brother Absalom."*

- **Traditional reading**: A gracious counterpoint to the hard justice of vv. 5-6. "To eat at the king's table" was the equivalent of having a royal pension — a regular allowance of food and clothing, with house and land (Wiseman, cited by Enduring Word). Barzillai had supplied David during his flight from Absalom (2 Samuel 17:27-29; 19:31-40). Chimham was likely the son of Barzillai (2 Samuel 19:37).
  - URL: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-2/
  - URL: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_kings/2.htm

- **Ellicott**: This charge "stands out in pleasant contrast." There is a reference in Jeremiah 41:17 to "the habitation of Chimham" near Bethlehem, suggesting David gave him inheritance there from his own patrimony.
  - URL: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_kings/2.htm

---

### v. 8 — *"Keep an eye on Shimei the son of Gera, the Benjamite from Bahurim who is with you. He called down bitter curses against me on the day I went to Mahanaim…"*

- **Traditional reading**: Shimei had cursed David during his flight from Absalom (2 Samuel 16:5-13) and later came to meet David at the Jordan seeking pardon (2 Samuel 19:18-23). David swore he would not put him to death.
  - URL: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-2/

- **Ellicott** calls this "the most ungenerous charge" — a virtual withdrawal of the pardon freely granted long before. It is "partly dictated by policy" (Shimei was powerful and represented the fallen house of Saul), but "there are unmistakable traces of the old grudge rankling in David's heart."
  - URL: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_kings/2.htm

- **Pulpit Commentary** takes a different view: David had realized that in a moment of generous enthusiasm he had pardoned what he had no power to pardon — blasphemy against the Lord's anointed, for which the Mosaic law attached the death penalty (Leviticus 24:14-16). Like unpunished murder, unpunished blasphemy defiled the land. David would keep his oath, but Solomon was under no such obligation. The charge is about justice, not grudge.
  - URL: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/1_kings/2.htm

- **Pulpit** also suggests Shimei may be the same Shimei mentioned in 1 Kings 1:8 as one who "was not with Adonijah" — a firm adherent of Solomon, wielding great influence with a thousand Benjamites (2 Samuel 19:17). If so, "thou hast with thee" accurately describes his position as a recent supporter.
  - URL: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/1_kings/2.htm

---

### v. 9 — *"Now therefore, do not hold him guiltless, for you are a wise man. You know what you ought to do to him to bring his gray head down to Sheol in blood."*

- **Traditional reading**: David does not specify the method — he trusts Solomon's wisdom. "Hold him not guiltless" means "do not leave him unpunished" (cf. Exodus 20:7; Jeremiah 30:11). David clearly desires that wisdom and justice, not malice or passion, guide Solomon.
  - URL: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/1_kings/2.htm

- **Enduring Word**: David knew he was right to keep his vow not to kill Shimei, but it was also right to ensure Shimei received justice without David breaking his vow. Solomon would need to find a just occasion.
  - URL: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-2/

---

### v. 10 — *"Then David rested with his fathers and was buried in the City of David."*

- **Traditional reading**: "Rested with his fathers" becomes a common phrase throughout 1 and 2 Kings for the passing of a king. David passed from this life to eternal rest and reward.
  - URL: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-2/

- **Enduring Word** quotes Trapp: "Of his adultery and murder we hear not a word, because he had made a thorough peace with God for those sins in his lifetime." Also Clarke: "In general he lived well, and it is most evident that he died well; and as a king, a general, a poet, a father, and a friend, he has had few equals, and no superior, from his own time to the present day."
  - URL: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-2/

- **Ellicott**: "Buried in the city of David" means Mount Zion. The "sepulchres of David" are noted in Nehemiah 3:16 and Ezekiel 43:7-9. They became the regular tombs of the kings.
  - URL: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_kings/2.htm

- **G. Campbell Morgan** (cited in Enduring Word): "With Solomon began, in some senses, the most splendid period in Israel's history. The splendor, however, was largely mental and material. The spiritual is noticeably absent."
  - URL: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-2/

---

### v. 11 — *"The length of David's reign over Israel was forty years—seven years in Hebron and thirty-three years in Jerusalem."*

- **Traditional reading**: A summary statement typical of the Deuteronomic historian. Forty years is a round, symbolic number in Scripture for a full generation or complete period of testing and rule.
  - (This is a straightforward historical note; no significant commentary disagreement was found.)

---

### v. 12 — *"So Solomon sat on the throne of his father David, and his kingdom was firmly established."*

- **Traditional reading**: This is phrased to show fulfillment of the promise in 2 Samuel 7:12-16 — a definite and partial fulfillment in Solomon, ultimately fulfilled in Jesus.
  - URL: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-2/

- **Ellicott**: The closing verse of the chapter (v. 46) shows that *after* the deaths and degradations, "the kingdom was established in the hand of Solomon." Under the smooth surface of apparent loyalty after David's death lurked some elements of disaffection and danger. The death of David was the signal for some attempts at rebellion in the conquered nations (1 Kings 11:14-25).
  - URL: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_kings/2.htm

---

### v. 13 — *"Now Adonijah son of Haggith went to Bathsheba the mother of Solomon, and she asked, 'Do you come in peace?' 'Yes, in peace,' he replied."*

- **Traditional reading**: Bathsheba's question was valid and pointed. Adonijah had attempted to seize the throne and was only spared on condition of good behavior (1 Kings 1:52). He had reason to wish revenge on Bathsheba, who (with Nathan) had exposed his plot to David.
  - URL: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-2/

- **Ellicott**: This illustrates the universal custom of Eastern monarchies — the king's mother held great dignity and influence, while the king's many wives were of little political account. Hence the name of each king's mother is constantly recorded.
  - URL: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_kings/2.htm

- **Precept Austin**: "Adonijah is deceiving Bathsheba for he still harbored hidden motives of usurping Solomon."
  - URL: https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-kings-2-commentary

---

### v. 14-15 — *"Then he said, 'I have something to tell you… You know that the kingship was mine… All Israel expected that I should reign, but the kingship has turned to my brother, for it has come to him from the LORD.'"*

- **Traditional reading**: Adonijah's words show craft — flattering Bathsheba by extolling her influence, and making a show of pious resignation ("it was his from the LORD"). In reality, he seems to suffer from delusions of grandeur: only a handful of malcontents supported him, and they quickly deserted (1 Kings 1:49).
  - URL: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-2/
  - URL: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_kings/2.htm

- **Ellicott**: He asserts, "in evident contradiction to fact," that the kingdom had been destined to him by popular desire.
  - URL: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_kings/2.htm

- **GotQuestions.org**: Adonijah was older than Solomon and therefore, under normal circumstances, in line before him. But God had promised Solomon the throne. Adonijah's followers had fled; Solomon mercifully granted him life on condition of homage and giving up his claim (1 Kings 1:52-53). Yet Adonijah was clearly not done.
  - URL: https://www.gotquestions.org/Solomon-Adonijah-Abishag.html

---

### v. 16-17 — *"So now I have just one request of you; do not deny me… Please speak to King Solomon, since he will not turn you down. Let him give me Abishag the Shunammite as my wife."*

- **Traditional reading**: Adonijah's request seems innocuous but is full of subterfuge. In the ancient Near East, taking a deceased king's concubines or harem was a declaration of the right to the throne. Absalom had done this when he rebelled against David (2 Samuel 16:20-23). Abishag, though never sexually intimate with David, was considered part of his harem. Adonijah wants to build a claim to Solomon's throne through this marriage.
  - URL: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-2/
  - URL: https://www.gotquestions.org/Solomon-Adonijah-Abishag.html

- **Precept Austin** (citing David O'Brien): Marriage to the right woman cemented claims to the throne. David himself had reclaimed Michal, Saul's daughter, to establish himself as Saul's heir. Adonijah is trying to link himself with the former regime through marriage.
  - URL: https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-kings-2-commentary

- **Ellicott**: The petition was "apparently harmless, and (since Abishag was concubine of David only in name) involving nothing unnatural," yet "had perhaps a covert design: for, by universal Eastern custom, to take a king's wives was the known privilege or duty of his successor."
  - URL: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_kings/2.htm

---

### v. 18 — *"'Very well,' Bathsheba replied. 'I will speak to the king for you.'"*

- **Traditional reading**: Bathsheba knew this was an outrageous request, but agreed to bring it to Solomon — probably believing it was best that Solomon know what Adonijah was plotting.
  - URL: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-2/

- **Ellicott** notes, strikingly, that Bathsheba "strangely enough, does not see" the political implications that Solomon sees immediately.
  - URL: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_kings/2.htm

---

### v. 19 — *"So Bathsheba went to King Solomon… The king stood up to greet her, bowed to her, and sat down on his throne. Then the king had a throne brought for his mother, who sat down at his right hand."*

- **Traditional reading**: Solomon showed his mother the highest honour. The queen mother, not the king's wife, held the place of greatest female dignity in the royal court. Having a throne set at his right hand was the position of highest honour and shared authority.
  - URL: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-2/

- **Ellicott**: These signs of honour contrast with Bathsheba's approach to David (1 Kings 1:15-16, 28, 31), where there is no trace of such ceremony. This illustrates how the king's mother was a person of great dignity in Eastern monarchies.
  - URL: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_kings/2.htm

---

### v. 20-21 — *"'I have just one small request of you,' she said… 'Let Abishag the Shunammite be given to your brother Adonijah as his wife.'"*

- **Traditional reading**: Bathsheba calls it "one small petition" — she was at least a little sarcastic, knowing it was not small at all, to make Adonijah's request seem even more offensive to Solomon. Solomon had already promised not to refuse her before hearing the request.
  - URL: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-2/

---

### v. 22 — *"King Solomon answered his mother, 'Why do you request Abishag the Shunammite for Adonijah? Since he is my older brother, you might as well request the kingdom for him and for Abiathar the priest and for Joab son of Zeruiah!'"*

- **Traditional reading**: Solomon understood the situation perfectly. He immediately recognized this as Adonijah's attempt to claim the throne. By mentioning Abiathar and Joab, Solomon shows he knows the old conspiracy is still alive — these were Adonijah's key supporters (1 Kings 1:7).
  - URL: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-2/
  - URL: https://www.gotquestions.org/Solomon-Adonijah-Abishag.html

- **Ellicott** detects a certain bitterness in Solomon's answer, "venting itself in irony," suggesting "some passionate feeling, not unlike the bursts of passion in his father, as in the case of Nabal (1 Samuel 25:21-22)." Ellicott then raises an interesting conjecture: that Abishag was the "fair Shulamite" of the Song of Solomon, already loved by the youthful king, adding a personal dimension to his wrath. He infers the hand of conspirators and "executes vengeance accordingly, summarily and without giving them any trial or opportunity of excusing themselves."
  - URL: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_kings/2.htm

---

### v. 23 — *"Then King Solomon swore by the LORD: 'May God punish me, and ever so severely, if Adonijah has not made this request at the expense of his life.'"*

- **Traditional reading**: "May God do so to me, and more also" is a well-known Hebrew imprecation formula (cf. Ruth 1:17; 1 Samuel 3:17; 14:44; 20:13; 25:22). The LXX renders it, "May God do these things to me and add these things also." It was probably accompanied by some gesture signifying utter destruction.
  - URL: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_kings/2.htm

- **Solomon's reasoning**: He acted according to the "terms of parole" granted to Adonijah in 1 Kings 1:52 — "If he proves himself a worthy man, not one hair of him shall fall to the earth; but if wickedness is found in him, he shall die." Adonijah made a treasonous request and is executed for it.
  - URL: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-2/

- **GotQuestions.org**: The tension was longstanding. Adonijah was older; under normal circumstances the throne was his. But God appointed Solomon. Adonijah had already been shown mercy once. His ongoing attempt to become king led to his early and abrupt death. "We are called to submit to God's will and to live contentedly where God has placed us in life."
  - URL: https://www.gotquestions.org/Solomon-Adonijah-Abishag.html

- **Ellicott** also contrasts Solomon's adjuration with David's in 1 Kings 1:29: "In David we always see the living man, whose soul longs after God with a vivid personal devotion. Solomon is emphatically the king, sitting on the throne of David, with his house established for ever. In the majesty of his royalty his individual character is to us almost entirely merged."
  - URL: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_kings/2.htm

---

## Points of Divergence Among Traditions

### On v. 4 (The Conditional Davidic Covenant)

- **Reformed/Baptist (John Piper, Desiring God)** : Stresses that the conditionality proves the covenant's ultimate fulfillment required a perfectly obedient Son — Christ. The promise was absolute regarding the Messiah; conditional regarding temporal kings.
  - URL: https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/gods-covenant-with-david

- **Matthew Henry (Puritan/Evangelical)** : Similarly distinguishes an absolute promise of the Messiah from the conditional promise of temporal succession.
  - URL: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/mhn/1-kings-2.html

- **Pentecostal/Charismatic (Enduring Word / David Guzik)** : Emphasizes the application to believers — we have a parallel promise in Matthew 6:33 ("seek first the kingdom"). Focuses on practical obedient fellowship with God as the ground of blessing, without extensive discussion of covenant theology distinctions.
  - URL: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-2/

### On David's Charge to Execute Joab and Shimei (vv. 5-9)

- **Anglican (Ellicott)** : Sees David's words as "singularly true to imperfect human nature, although utterly unworthy of an ideal picture of a hero-king." Finds "worldly prudence of the old statesman" and "long-remembered grudge," especially regarding Shimei. The charge against Shimei "cannot stand examination on the ground of equity or generosity."
  - URL: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_kings/2.htm

- **Pulpit Commentary (more conservative)** : Vigorously defends David against charges of vindictiveness. Under the Mosaic *lex talionis*, the king had no discretion to pardon murder or blasphemy. David was enforcing covenantal justice, not personal revenge. The land itself would be defiled (Numbers 35:33). The famine for the Gibeonites (2 Samuel 21:1) had proven this principle.
  - URL: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/1_kings/2.htm

- **Enduring Word (David Guzik, Pentecostal)** : Takes a middle ground. Acknowledges the complexity of Joab's character (fiercely loyal yet not obedient) and the possibility that Joab blackmailed David over Uriah. Treats David's instructions as a matter of justice that David was personally unable to carry out — whether from weakness, obligation, or political impossibility.
  - URL: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-2/

### On Adonijah's Execution (vv. 22-25)

- **Evangelical (GotQuestions.org)** : Straightforward reading — Adonijah's request was a treasonous power-grab using ancient harem customs. Solomon was justified in executing him under the terms of the earlier parole (1 Kings 1:52). God appoints rulers; rebellion brings consequences.
  - URL: https://www.gotquestions.org/Solomon-Adonijah-Abishag.html

- **Anglican (Ellicott)** : More nuanced — Solomon's response betrays "passionate feeling" and he executes Adonijah "summarily and without giving them any trial or opportunity of excusing themselves." Raises the conjecture that Abishag may have been the Shulamite of Song of Solomon, adding a personal (romantic) motive to Solomon's political judgment.
  - URL: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_kings/2.htm

---

## Other Views

- **Modern Scholarship (Abishag as the Shulamite)** : Both GotQuestions.org and Ellicott note the theory that Abishag the Shunammite may be the Shulamite woman of the Song of Solomon (Song 6:13), based on the similarity between "Shunammite" and "Shulamite." GotQuestions.org says "there is no solid biblical evidence for the link" but acknowledges it as "an interesting theory put forward by some scholars."
